title: Blue Mockingbird
summary: Blue Mockingbird is described in MITRE ATT&CK not as a formal organisation but as a cluster of observed activity centred on cryptocurrency mining payloads delivered in dynamic link library form on Windows systems, with the earliest observed tooling dated to December 2019. The shape of the activity is what makes it worth studying, because almost every step depends on a legitimate Windows component doing something it was never meant to do. Reported initial access is through a vulnerability in a third party web application component, which places the attacker inside the context of a web server process. From that starting point the activity escalates by abusing an impersonation privilege held by web application pool accounts, executes its payload through signed system utilities that load libraries, and then hides behind names copied from legitimate components of the operating system so that casual file name review looks clean. Persistence is layered: a Windows service, a scheduled task, and an event subscription that triggers execution when a specific event occurs. Further execution is arranged by setting an environment variable that makes any process loading the dotnet runtime pull in the attacker library, which is a durable and very broad execution hook. Credential theft from memory and interactive use of remote desktop and administrative file shares follow, so the operators are hands on rather than fully automated. The defensive takeaway is process lineage rather than file reputation: a web server process that spawns a command shell, or a signed system utility loading a library from a writeable directory, is a strong signal. The common misunderstanding is that hidden mining is minor because data was not stolen; here the same access includes credential theft, which supports whatever the operator wants next.

beginner.definition: Blue Mockingbird is the name for a set of activity that hides coin mining software on Windows servers. Researchers first saw the tools in late 2019. It gets in through a weakness in a web application component. Then it uses normal Windows programs to run its hidden software.
beginner.whyItMatters: The group does not stop at mining coins. It also steals passwords from the server memory. That means the same break in can lead to stolen data later. It hides its files behind names that match real Windows parts, so quick checks look clean. It also sets itself to restart in several ways at once. If you remove only one hidden program, the others bring it back. Treat it as a full intrusion, not a small problem.
howItWorks: The intruders find a web server running a component with a known weakness.
They exploit that weakness to run commands as the web server account.
They use a known trick to raise their rights to full system level.
They run hidden mining software through normal Windows programs, not obvious files.
They copy the name of a real Windows file so the harmful file looks familiar.
They add several ways to restart automatically, then steal passwords and move to other machines.
beginner.example: Imagine a cleaner who works in an office tower with a master key card. The card was issued for the storeroom only, but the lifts accept it everywhere. The cleaner wears a uniform with the building logo and carries a trolley labelled with a real department name. Nobody stops the trolley, because everything about it looks official. In the basement the cleaner plugs in a machine that runs all night. The building pays the electricity bill, and the same key card still opens the records room. Legitimate tools in the wrong hands are exactly this powerful.
takeaways: A trusted system program can be used to run harmful code, so watch what it loads.
Web servers should never need to start command shells for normal business.
Several different restart methods mean you must clean all of them, not just one.

objectives: Explain why this activity is described as a cluster of behaviour rather than a named organisation.
Describe how a web server process becomes the starting point of an intrusion.
Explain how a signed system utility or a runtime environment variable can be abused to run code.
Identify the persistence mechanisms that must all be removed during cleanup.
Recognise process lineage evidence that distinguishes legitimate administration from this activity.
